extracted.intended_audience: authors preparing manuscripts for submission to Conservation Biology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for preparing and formatting manuscripts (titles, abstract, sections, citations, tables/figures, language, statistics, and supporting information) for submission to the journal Conservation Biology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word count limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers must not exceed the following word counts ... The number of words includes all text from the first word of the Abstract through the last word of Literature Cited; it does not include tables or figure legends or text in the body of tables. The Abstract must not exceed 300 words. Do not include an abstract with Letters, Comments, or Diversity pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributed Papers: 6000 words; Research Notes: 3000 words; Reviews: 7500 words; Essays: 6000 words; Conservation Practice and Policy: 5000 words; Comments: 2000 words; Diversity: 2000 words; Letters: 1000 words. Papers must not exceed these counts even if reviewers request additional material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of counted text
rubrics_metrics.description: Word count includes all text from the first word of the Abstract through the last word of Literature Cited; excludes tables, figure legends, and text in the body of tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of tables and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Include no more than one supporting element (i.e., table or figure) for every four pages of text (from the Abstract through the Literature Cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a table or figure has only a few data points, incorporate the data into the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendices and supporting information policy
rubrics_metrics.description: We rarely allow appendices in the print version of the journal. Supplementary data or method details typically should be provided as online Supporting Information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See supporting information section for citation format and responsibilities for content/functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required manuscript sections and order
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributed Papers, Research Notes, and Conservation Practice and Policy papers should contain the following sections in the following order: Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, Supporting Information paragraph (if there are online appendices), Literature Cited, tables, figure legends, and figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not combine sections (e.g., Results and Discussion). Do not number section headings or subheadings. Do not include a Conclusion section (conclusions are part of the Discussion). The Acknowledgements section will be added after acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title: clarity and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles should be clear and concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use hanging titles (those with a colon or dash), titles that are complete sentences, interrogative titles, and titles that reference colloquialisms or popular culture. Avoid sensationalism; titles should reflect the content well and be immediately clear to readers and indexing services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract content and format
rubrics_metrics.description: The Abstract should summarize the Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion in that order (i.e., it should be a mini-version of the paper). Key points from each of these sections should be identifiable within the Abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the top of the abstract page provide the title of the paper. The Abstract should not include literature citations, much data, or phrases such as 'We discuss . . .' or 'We summarize . . .' Maximum 300 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keywords
rubrics_metrics.description: Include on the cover page five to eight words or phrases that will be useful for indexing and literature searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid general terms such as conservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgments placement and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the acknowledgment paragraph on the cover page of your manuscript. (Reviewers are not provided with a cover page.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not spell out first names; provide first initial only. Do not use titles (Dr., Professor). Refer to authors of the manuscript by their initials only (e.g., 'S.T.W. was supported by a grant from the Torry Foundation.').

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes in body
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use footnotes in the body of the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-text citation format and ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: In the body of the paper order citations from oldest to newest and use name-year format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cite work or data that have not been published or are not available; include such work or data as online Supporting Information and cite it as such. If data is available in a publicly accessible database, you may cite that database and include databases in Literature Cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature Cited: journal titles and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the full names of all journal titles. Do not italicize titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature Cited: long author lists
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are more than 10 authors, use et al. (Howard, G., et al.) instead of listing the names of all authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature Cited exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers in review and personal communications should not be included in the Literature Cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceedings and abstracts citation rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings and abstracts from conferences may be cited only if they have a 'publisher' and the location of the publisher (or the organization from which the document may be obtained) can be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example citation formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide specific examples for journal articles, edited books, reports, and online journals (with and without DOI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a paper is in press, the 'in press' follows the volume number. No access dates needed for online journals with stable URLs; include DOI when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet sources other than journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the name of the organization hosting the website, their geographical location, and an access date (month year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: Carne, A. 2003. Ranges of endangered Colombian birds. BirdLife International, Cambridge, United Kingdom. Available from http:... (accessed March 2014).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing in-press manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Officially accepted manuscripts may be cited as in press in Literature Cited (….Conservation Biology: in press.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In text, provide year of publication (e.g., Stevens 2015). In Literature Cited provide the volume number and substitute 'in press' for page numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting elements should supplement, not duplicate text
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables and figures should be self-explanatory and should supplement rather than duplicate the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present large amounts of data in tables. A reader should be able to interpret tables and figures without referring to the text. Define all abbreviations and terms unique to the paper in the figure legend or table caption or footnotes. Common statistical notations need not be defined. Use the same terminology in supporting elements and in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to cite supporting elements in text
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a summary or generalization of results and cite supporting elements parenthetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use phrasing such as 'Models for species abundance were significant and explained 78% to 92% of variability (Table 2),' rather than 'Table 2 shows the outcome of models...'. Abbreviate 'Fig.' unless figure is the first word in a sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table legends and footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Legends should be one sentence long and describe the contents of the table as it relates to the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A list of the table’s columns or row headings is not an informative legend. Use footnotes for detailed descriptions, to define terms, and to define abbreviations. Define abbreviations in a footnote even if already defined in text. If only one footnote use an asterisk (*); if more than one use letters (a, b, c). Order footnotes alphabetically from left to right and top to bottom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table formatting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use bold type. Do not use grid lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless an entry is a complete sentence or a proper noun, capitalize only the first word of the first entry in a row and do not use periods. Do not split tables into separate sections (e.g., Table 1a and Table 1b); make separate tables or combine data. Use indentation to set off secondary or tertiary entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure file formats and resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures must be of sufficient quality and resolution to remain clear at 60% reduction. Before publication, supply figures in tif, eps, or pdf format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolution should be at least 300 dpi; 600 dpi preferable for figures with lettering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color figure policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Conservation Biology cannot waive charges for printing of color figures ($700/page). We discourage the use of color because in some countries download speeds are slow and gray-scale photocopies are common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may have color figures in the online version and gray-scale in print. Reference to color cannot be made in the figure legend or text and elements in the gray-scale version must be distinguishable. Supply separate files for color and gray-scale figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure legends placement
rubrics_metrics.description: The legends for all figures should be grouped on a page that precedes the figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not place a figure and its legend on the same page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps: scale bars and compass
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale bars and compass direction must be provided for maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph labeling and design
rubrics_metrics.description: Label all axes and include units of measure in the label.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize the first letter of axis labels. Include a key in the figure rather than describing shading or shapes in the legend. Match typeface and type size among figures. For multi-panel figures use lowercase letters (a), (b), (c) and reference each panel by letter in the legend. If many digits/long descriptions along x-axis, orient entries at 45° or fewer. All numbers along an axis must have the same number of significant figures. Y-axis label oriented vertically left (reading bottom to top); numerals horizontally oriented. Center labels along axes. Do not enclose graphs in a rectangle. Do not use color on a figure that will be published in gray scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting Information citation paragraph format
rubrics_metrics.description: Before Literature Cited, insert a paragraph in the exact format shown that provides a brief description of supporting information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Supporting Information: XXX (Appendix S1), XXX (Appendix S2), and a XXX translation of the article (Appendix S3) are available online. The authors are solely responsible for the content and functionality of these materials. Queries (other than absence of the material) should be directed to the corresponding author.' Every piece is cited as Supporting Information, not by specific number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Our audience is broad and international. Clarity in language and syntax is important, especially for readers whose first language is not English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jargon and colloquialisms. If English is not your first language, ask a native English speaker with publishing experience to proofread the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology: define ambiguous terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some common terms in conservation science have multiple meanings (e.g., biological diversity, wildlife, connectivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify how you use such terms, and define specialized terms at first use in the Abstract and in the body of the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations and acronyms rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not begin a sentence with an abbreviation. Use abbreviations sparingly. Define all abbreviations, initializations, and acronyms at first use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: analysis of variance (ANOVA), International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic designations: Do not capitalize a term that indicates region unless it is being used as a proper noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for preferred capitalization (e.g., western states, Southeast Asia). Threat categories used by authoritative bodies should not be capitalized (threatened, endangered, critically endangered, conservation concern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Active voice preference
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, use we or I (i.e., active voice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods should not be written entirely in passive voice. Example: 'We converted all GIS data to raster format.' rather than 'All GIS data were converted...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use past tense in the Methods, Results, and in the Discussion (referring to your results). Use present tense when you refer to published results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: in attribution/presentation it is correct to say, e.g., 'Toffel (2008) found [past] that extracts from iron weed inhibit [present] fungal growth.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding dangling participles and misplaced modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'using' often causes dangling participles and misplaced modifiers. Be careful with sentence constructions that imply the wrong agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of bad and better sentences provided. Also avoid multiple adjectival nouns; prefer 'trade in African elephant ivory' to 'African elephant ivory trade.' Use 'affected', not 'impacted.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Split infinitives and pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Splitting an infinitive can be useful for emphasis or readability; sentences should not sound awkward because of avoiding a split infinitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with pronouns this, these, and it; provide qualifiers to make antecedents clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthetical versus narrative citations and ampersand usage
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, enclose citations in text in parentheses. Use an ampersand (&) between author surnames when the citation is parenthetical; when a citation is not parenthetical, use 'and'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example parenthetical: (Bird & Sanchez 2010). Narrative: 'Our results are consistent with the predictions of Wolf and Rhymer (2011).' For >2 authors use et al. (Hatchwell et al. 1996). List parenthetical citations chronologically and separate multiple entries with semicolons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting 'in press' and unpublished data citations
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In press' means the cited paper has been accepted unconditionally for publication. Provide the year of publication in the text and 'in press' in Literature Cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use initials for unpublished data held by authors of the paper: (C.S.C. & L.K., unpublished data). Use initial for first name and full surname for other sources: (R. Fowler, unpublished data; M.E. Cortez, personal communication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software and trademarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Software: capitalize the first letter only if the name of the program is a word; if not, use all capital letters (e.g., SAS). Do not use trademark symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that all references cited in text are listed in the Literature Cited and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'in. lit.' citations. Provide original citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers, units, and statistical reporting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow Scientific Style and Format, 7th edition. Most numbers in most circumstances, even those under 10, appear as numerals (exceptions handled by copyeditors). Decimal point: insert 0 before a decimal point (0.4, not .4). Use symbols for percentages and degrees (15%, 15°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fractions may be spelled out unless used with units of measure. Report calculated values to not more than one significant digit beyond measurement accuracy; report test statistics (p values, correlation coefficients) to not more than 3 significant digits. SD and SE formatting examples provided (do not use ±). Dates: day, month, year (e.g., 6 October 1987). Insert a space between numbers and unit (6 m, 14 mL). Avoid numbered lists in text. Delimiters ordering in math: braces { }, brackets [ ], parentheses ( ) for mathematical expressions; define variables in equations; italicize single-letter variables; do not italicize multi-letter variables or words used with variables; complete-word variables lowercase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations for statistical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the following abbreviations: p, probability; df, degrees of freedom; χ2, chi-square; F (F test, variance ratio); FST; CI, confidence interval or credible interval; SE, standard error; SD, standard deviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use ± with SE or SD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific names and common names formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: English and scientific names of birds should follow the checklist of the International Ornithological Congress; deviations must be supported by explicit citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common names of taxonomic groups other than birds should be in lower case. In the abstract and at first mention use common name followed by scientific name in parentheses: cane toad (Bufo marinus). Thereafter, after scientific name has been provided use common name. For organisms: Clarkia springvillensis (first use); C. springvillensis thereafter (even starting a sentence); spp. or sp. or var. (no italics).
